You lower the brass cap without fastening it. The pressure beneath it lifts the edge once, lightly, against your thumb.

“Five minutes,” you tell Nessa. “I need to see the light safe.”

She draws breath to object, then glances up at the machinery. “Five of yours, or five ordinary ones?”

“Bring your bag upstairs. You can count.”

The iron stair rings beneath your boots. Above the kitchen’s warmth, the tower smells of oil and damp whitewash; narrow windows admit strips of grey sea. Nessa follows close enough that you hear her breathing change on the last turn. In the lantern room, the great lens gathers your small flame into curved, multiplying reflections. Beyond the glass, a fishing boat moves toward the harbour mouth with scarcely enough sail to give it shape against the mist.

You check the oil feed, the burner, the governor. Familiar work steadies your hands. The mechanism turns cleanly, and the reserve vessel holds enough for the night. You make the entry in the station book, including the time of the three notes. Beside it you write *heard through lower speaking tube*. Your pen pauses before the word *bell*.

“Why leave that out?” Nessa asks.

“Because I heard three notes. I haven’t seen what made them.”

She rubs a wet cuff between her palms. “Put that they frightened me, then. You’ve seen that.”

You look at her. She meets your eyes without smiling. Beneath the observation, you add her name as witness.

By the time you pocket the letter and its tracing, the clock’s minute hand has moved six divisions. Nessa notices, but says nothing.

Outside, rain has thinned to a fine spray that settles on your coat rather than falling. The headland road gleams between its low walls. You carry the lamp hooded against the wind, its handle awkward beneath your crooked fingers, while Nessa walks on the seaward side and watches the roofs below.

“Anyone else have a key to your store?” you ask.

“Iven borrowed it when he did the door. Gave it back.” She takes a shorter step where water crosses the road. “And I keep a spare at home. Before you ask, my children know better than to play down there.”

“I wasn’t going to ask that.”

“You were going to ask something with the same face.”

At the fish market, two men stack trestles beneath the arcade. A woman shakes scales from a canvas apron into the gutter. Nessa calls to her that you are looking at the cellar; the woman raises a hand, then resumes shaking. The ordinary movement offers a comfort you distrust yourself for needing.

Nessa’s storeroom opens with a swollen scrape. Inside, salt sacks lean against one wall, and empty fish boxes give off a sour, woody smell. She shifts a handcart, exposing a narrow stair behind it. Your lamp finds shallow stone treads descending into darkness.

You stop on the threshold. **There are seven.**

Nessa takes a length of packing cord from a peg and knots it around the outside door handle, holding the door open against its tendency to swing shut.

“That stays,” she says.

You descend sideways, keeping your shoulder clear of the wall. The bottom tread is dry beneath a skin of pale grit. At its edge lies a recent-looking smear, as though something wet has been dragged across the stone and lifted away.

The door beyond is older than the frame enclosing it. Last winter’s mortar forms a rough band around three sides, but along the hinge edge a dark slit runs from floor to lintel. Set into the wall beside it is a brass pipe mouth, green with corrosion.

Nessa crouches on the step above you. “It wasn’t cracked on Monday.”

You bring the lamp closer. The mortar has broken into small flakes on your side; several still hang by threads of lime. Near the latch, a clean patch interrupts the grime at the height of a human palm.

Then the latch moves.

Only a fraction. Enough to scrape iron against iron.

Nessa grips the back of your coat. From somewhere in the connected stone comes a voice, faint but distinct.

“Keep clear of the door.”

You cannot tell whether the speaker stands immediately beyond it. Beneath the sill, a thin line of water begins to darken the dust.
